name: Face slimming supplements / teas

angle.text: Users take herbal slimming teas and capsules hoping for a leaner, less puffy face, often through diuretic, laxative or detox effects. No trial has tested them for facial fat, and the appearance link rests on general weight-loss marketing and anecdote.

summary: Herbal teas and capsules sold for a slimmer face; no trial has tested them for facial fat and some herbal slimming ingredients have been banned.
note: Herbal products are not required to show efficacy in the US; some ingredients have drug interactions or were withdrawn.
currentQuick:
Face slimming teas and supplements are herbal products promoted for reducing puffiness or facial fat, often with diuretic or detox claims.
No trial found has tested them for the face. Encyclopedic sources note that US herbal teas need only be safe, not proven effective.
How it works: Marketing cites water loss, appetite suppression or faster metabolism. Research on spot reduction generally reports that fat loss is not targeted to one body area.
Risks and caveats: Documented concerns include contamination, drug interactions with some herbs, and past bans such as ephedra in 2004. Individual products vary widely.
deepLead:
Face slimming supplements and teas are herbal products marketed or discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness or fat, usually through claims of diuretic, laxative, metabolism-boosting or detox effects. They are sold under the broader heading of herbal and dietary weight-loss products.
In the United States, herbal teas are treated as food products that must be safe to consume but are not required to show evidence of efficacy. No published human trial found in the sources reviewed has tested any tea or supplement specifically for reducing facial fat.
Documented safety concerns with weight-loss herbal products include contamination and drug interactions with some herbs, and the 2004 US ban of ephedra-containing supplements.

name: Ketogenic diet face

chain: Fat loss and less water retention
angle.text: Appearance communities use a ketogenic diet to lean out the cheeks and reduce puffiness, via overall fat loss and lower water retention. Weight-loss studies exist for the diet, while the face specifically has not been studied.

summary: Keto for a leaner face: a real diet with epilepsy origins; weight-loss advantage is small and no study covers the face.
note: Associated with constipation, raised cholesterol and rare ketoacidosis; contraindicated in some metabolic disorders.
currentQuick:
Some people say a ketogenic diet slims the face by cutting bloat and body fat.
The diet was created for epilepsy in the 1920s. For weight loss, a 2022 Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found no benefit over balanced diets at two years, and no study measures facial effects.
How it works: Restricting carbohydrate drives the liver to make ketone bodies for fuel. Researchers attribute most weight loss on such diets to reduced calorie intake.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include constipation, raised cholesterol, nutrient gaps and, rarely, ketoacidosis. It is contraindicated in certain metabolic disorders.
deepLead:
The ketogenic diet face refers to the belief in appearance communities that a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat ketogenic diet leans out the face, reducing puffiness and cheek fat. The diet itself restricts carbohydrate so that the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel, and was developed in the 1920s as a treatment for epilepsy.
Low-carbohydrate diets can produce somewhat greater short-term weight loss than low-fat diets, but a 2022 Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found no benefit over balanced diets at two years. No published trial found in the sources reviewed has measured facial fat or facial appearance on a ketogenic diet.

name: OMAD / 36-hour fasts

angle.text: Looksmaxxing users eat one meal a day or fast for 36 hours to lose body fat quickly and reveal a leaner face. Intermittent fasting has modest trial evidence for weight loss, while facial leanness from these protocols rests on anecdote.

summary: One meal a day or 36-hour fasts for fast fat loss; intermittent fasting has modest evidence and health bodies call it inconclusive.
note: Not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders; some lean mass is lost.
currentQuick:
OMAD packs all eating into one meal; 36-hour fasts leave a day and a half between meals. Forum users use them to cut fat and sometimes to reduce bloating.
Reviews show intermittent fasting can produce weight loss similar to calorie restriction in some studies, but health bodies describe the evidence as limited.
How it works: The pattern mainly lowers calorie intake. Weight lost includes fat and some lean mass.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include hunger, dizziness, headaches and irritability. Fasting is not recommended for several groups, and prolonged fasts raise gallstone risk.
deepLead:
OMAD (one meal a day) is a form of time-restricted eating in which all daily food is eaten in a window of one to two hours; 36-hour fasts extend the pause between meals beyond a day. Both are used in looksmaxxing communities to lose body fat quickly and get a leaner face.
Encyclopedic sources report that evidence for intermittent fasting matching calorie restriction is limited, with most human studies showing weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent. Health bodies including the American Heart Association and the US National Institute on Aging have described the evidence as limited or inconclusive.

name: Cardio / zone 2 for leanness

angle.text: Users do low-intensity steady cardio to burn calories and lower body fat, aiming for a leaner face and body. Aerobic exercise is well studied for health and weight, while zone 2 specifically for leanness is still debated.

summary: Steady aerobic exercise for fat loss; well-established for health, with zone 2 specifically still debated for leanness.
note: Fat loss is not site-specific; overuse injury and under-fuelling are reported risks.
currentQuick:
Looksmaxxers use steady cardio, often at zone 2 intensity, to drop body fat and look leaner, including in the face.
Aerobic exercise is reported to promote weight loss, though sources say high-intensity work can match benefits in less time and no trial targets facial leanness.
How it works: Low-intensity exercise relies mainly on fat for fuel. Researchers describe fat loss as a whole-body result of energy balance rather than something targeted to one area.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include overuse injury, overtraining and low-energy-availability problems in high-volume athletes.
deepLead:
Cardio for leanness is the use of aerobic exercise, including low-intensity steady-state work often called zone 2, to lose body fat and look leaner. Zone 2 has no universally accepted definition but is commonly placed at roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate, where fat is the main fuel and lactate is cleared about as fast as it is produced.
Public-health bodies recommend about 2.5 hours of moderate aerobic exercise per week for health, and sources report that aerobic exercise promotes weight loss. Encyclopedic sources note that aerobic exercise also has other benefits, and that high-intensity interval training can deliver similar benefits in less time.

name: Water fasting

angle.text: Users fast on water for days to drop body fat quickly and get facial leanness, with some claims about skin as well. Fasting studies cover weight and metabolic markers, while the skin and face claims rest on anecdote.

summary: Multi-day zero-calorie fasting for fast fat loss; documented risks include refeeding syndrome and loss of lean tissue.
note: Refeeding syndrome can be fatal and can occur after about 4 to 5 days without food.
currentQuick:
Water fasting means no calories for a day or more. Forum users use it for rapid fat loss and say it improves skin, and some report hair shedding afterward.
Physiology sources report a large share of early weight loss is lean tissue, and studies cover shorter intermittent fasts rather than repeated extended ones.
How it works: With no intake, the body uses glycogen and then protein and fat, shifting toward ketone use for the brain over days.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include electrolyte loss, gallstones and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal. Fasting is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders.
deepLead:
Water fasting, also called extended or zero-calorie fasting, is abstaining from all food and caloric drinks for 24 hours or more, usually several days. In looksmaxxing communities it is used for rapid fat loss and with claims about skin and facial leanness.
Physiology sources report that early weight loss in a prolonged fast includes a large share of lean tissue, and that the body later shifts toward ketosis. Documented risks include electrolyte disturbances, gallstones and refeeding syndrome.

name: T3 / thyroid fat loss

angle.text: Users take the thyroid hormone T3 off-label during cutting phases to raise metabolism and shed body fat. The drug is studied and approved for hypothyroidism, not for weight loss, so the appearance use is off-label and based mostly on bodybuilding anecdote.

summary: Using the thyroid hormone liothyronine (T3) off-label to cut body fat; the drug label says it is ineffective for weight loss at normal doses and risky at high ones.
note: The prescribing label warns that larger doses in people with normal thyroid function can cause serious toxicity.
currentQuick:
T3 is the active thyroid hormone, available by prescription as liothyronine for hypothyroidism. In bodybuilding and cutting circles it has been used off-label in the hope of raising metabolic rate and losing fat.
There is little looksmaxxing-specific documentation. The regulatory label states that, in people with normal thyroid function, ordinary hormone-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction.
How it works: T3 raises basal metabolic rate, affects protein synthesis and increases sensitivity to catecholamines such as adrenaline.
Risks and caveats: Excess thyroid hormone can cause sweating, tremor, insomnia, arrhythmias and heart failure. The label warns of serious or life-threatening toxicity at larger doses, especially alongside sympathomimetic amines. It is prescription-only in the UK and Canada.
deepLead:
Liothyronine is a synthetic form of triiodothyronine (T3), the more active of the two main thyroid hormones. It was approved for medical use in 1956 and is used mainly for hypothyroidism and myxedema coma.
In this entry, 'T3 thyroid fat loss' refers to the practice of taking thyroid hormone, without a thyroid disorder, in an attempt to speed fat loss during a cut. The prescribing information for liothyronine states that in people with normal thyroid function, normal-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses can be seriously toxic.
No published trial of T3 as a looksmaxxing or cosmetic fat-loss method was found.

name: Ephedrine / ECA stack

angle.text: Bodybuilders and looksmaxxers use the ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin stack to raise metabolism and curb appetite when cutting. Trials have found modest short-term fat loss, and guides pair it with exercise for a leaner physique.

summary: A stimulant combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used for cutting; trials show modest short-term fat loss with cardiovascular risk.
note: Ephedrine alkaloid supplements are illegal to market in the US; a forum guide itself warns against use with heart problems.
currentQuick:
ECA stands for ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It has long been popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions, and a looksmax.org guide describes it as a stack for raising metabolism, suppressing appetite and adding energy.
A 2021 systematic review found ephedrine, with or without caffeine, produced about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over 4 to 24 weeks. Long-term effects are unknown.
How it works: Ephedrine triggers release of norepinephrine, activating adrenergic receptors; it also slows gastric emptying. Caffeine and related methylxanthines are reported to act synergistically with it.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, tremor, rapid heart rate, arrhythmias and hypertension; stroke and heart attack are serious risks. The FDA banned ephedrine alkaloid supplements in 2004, and legal status varies by country.
deepLead:
The ECA stack combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. It is described as popular with bodybuilders cutting fat before competitions. A looksmax.org guide describes it as a stack for metabolism increase, appetite suppression and energy, to assist weight loss.
Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant that works mainly by triggering norepinephrine release. It produces modest short-term fat loss, and its long-term effects are unknown.

name: DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol)

angle.text: Some forum users pursue DNP, an industrial uncoupler, for very fast fat loss over a few weeks and an extremely lean look. It was marketed for weight loss in the 1930s, and current use is off-label and documented mainly through anecdote and case reports.

summary: An industrial mitochondrial uncoupler that burns fat as heat, banned for human use since 1938 and tied to documented deaths.
note: No antidote exists; overdose causes fatal hyperthermia, and UK regulators classify it as a poison.
currentQuick:
DNP is an industrial chemical that was sold as a diet drug in the 1930s and withdrawn after reports of cataracts, blindness and deaths. It has resurfaced online, where bodybuilders and others discussing fast fat loss on looksmaxxing forums describe taking it to cut weight.
Users on forums report rapid weight loss over a few weeks, alongside heat, sweating and fever. Regulators and clinicians describe it as having a narrow gap between effective and toxic exposure.
How it works: DNP acts as a protonophore: it lets protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, so energy that would have made ATP is released as heat and metabolic rate rises.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include dangerously high body temperature, cataracts, nerve damage and death, with no specific antidote. It is banned for human consumption in many countries, prohibited by WADA since 2015, and was reclassified as a regulated poison in the UK in 2023.
deepLead:
2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is an industrial chemical that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, converting food energy into heat rather than stored chemical energy. It was marketed as a weight-loss drug in the United States in the 1930s and was judged too toxic for human consumption under the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, DNP is discussed as a short-term fat-loss agent for cutting. Users on looksmax.org describe multi-week courses with large reported weight losses, often combined with other substances. Clinicians and regulators describe it as having a low therapeutic index and documented fatalities.
No published clinical trial has tested DNP as an appearance or weight-loss treatment in modern times. Evidence about its effects in humans comes mainly from 1930s clinical reports, toxicology and poison-centre case data.

name: Fat grafting for facial asymmetry

angle.text: Surgeons move a patient's own fat into the thinner side of the face so the two sides match in volume, giving a visibly fuller, more balanced face. Fat transfer is a standard reconstructive and aesthetic technique, with graft survival varying between patients.

summary: Moving a patient's own fat into the leaner side of the face to even out volume; common in surgery, but graft survival is unpredictable.
note: Reviews describe high and unpredictable fat absorption, so results may need repeat sessions.
currentQuick:
Fat grafting harvests fat, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas lacking volume. In looksmaxxing discussions it is cited as a way to build up a thinner side of the face.
Facial fat grafting is widely used in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery, but the studies reviewed here concern facial volume restoration in general, not asymmetry as such.
How it works: Harvested fat is washed or filtered and re-injected into target areas. Part of the graft is absorbed by the body, so surgeons judge retention from experience, according to a systematic review.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, fat necrosis and reabsorption; a systematic review asks whether facial fat grafting is worth its risk.
deepLead:
Fat grafting, or fat transfer, moves a person's own fat from one area to another. It has three stages: harvesting, usually by liposuction, processing, and reinjection. It is used in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery for volume replacement, including the face.
Fat grafting for facial asymmetry refers to using the technique to add volume to a deficient side so the two sides match. A systematic review reports that the main drawbacks of facial autologous fat grafting are high absorption and unpredictable volume retention.

name: Ptosis surgery for asymmetry

angle.text: Eyelid surgery lifts a lower-set upper lid so both eyes look more alike and more open. It is an established procedure for ptosis, and the change is visible once healed.

summary: Eyelid-lifting surgery to correct a drooping upper lid so the eyes match; an established procedure, with uneven lids a recognised complication.
note: Evidence covers ptosis repair generally; asymmetry results can recur or be uneven after surgery.
currentQuick:
Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid. Surgery tightens or replaces the lifting mechanism, and in looksmaxxing discussions it is cited as a way to make a droopy lid match the other eye.
Surgical series describe it as an established treatment for mild to severe ptosis, but outcomes vary by cause and technique.
How it works: Techniques include shortening the levator muscle, resecting Muller's muscle, or suspending the lid from the forehead muscle (frontalis sling) when the lid muscle is very weak.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include uneven lids after surgery, dry eye if the eye does not close fully, bleeding, infection, rarely loss of lid movement, and recurrence.
deepLead:
Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid, caused by dysfunction of the levator muscle, its nerve supply, or the sympathetic supply to Muller's muscle. Causes include aging, congenital factors, trauma and underlying conditions such as myasthenia gravis. Ptosis surgery for asymmetry refers to repairing a lower-set lid so that the two eyes look more alike.
Surgical options include levator resection, Muller's muscle resection and frontalis or Whitnall slings. Published case series of minimally invasive suspension techniques report correction of mild and moderate ptosis with short recovery.

name: Bilateral chewing habit

angle.text: Users alternate the chewing side in the hope of keeping jaw muscles and face shape even from left to right. The link from chewing side to facial symmetry is a community theory, and no studies were found on it.

summary: Deliberately alternating the chewing side in the hope of keeping the jaw and face symmetrical; no studies found on the claim.
note: Little published material addresses this practice in looksmaxxing terms.
currentQuick:
The practice is to chew evenly on both sides of the mouth rather than favouring one, on the premise that one-sided chewing could contribute to facial asymmetry.
No studies were found testing that premise.
How it works: Chewing is largely unconscious, though conscious input can influence it, and the pattern adapts to food and to changes in the teeth.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms were found for this practice.
deepLead:
The bilateral chewing habit is the practice of alternating the side used for chewing. Chewing is mostly unconscious, but conscious input can influence it, and feedback from nerves in the teeth and jaw joints helps control how long and how forcefully each muscle acts.
The pattern of chewing adapts to the type of food and to changes in the teeth, such as tooth loss or dentures.
No studies found linking habitual chewing side to facial asymmetry, and no authoritative source was found documenting how looksmaxxing communities discuss the practice.

name: Unilateral chewing correction

angle.text: People who chew mostly on one side try to use both sides, believing the habit contributes to a lopsided jaw and face. It is a free habit change, and the cause-and-effect link to asymmetry is untested.

summary: Deliberately chewing on both sides to fix a one-sided habit people blame for facial asymmetry; the cause-and-effect link is untested.
note: Studies describe chewing-side preference and its correlates, but none shows that changing it alters facial symmetry.
currentQuick:
Unilateral chewing correction means consciously alternating the side of the mouth used for chewing, or favouring the less-used side, to reduce a habit of chewing mostly on one side. In looksmaxxing circles the habit is sometimes blamed for uneven jaw or cheek development.
Research confirms that most people have a preferred chewing side and has studied how it relates to handedness, bite pattern and jaw disorders. No published study has tested whether correcting the habit changes facial appearance.
How it works: The proposed idea is that the chewing-side masseter and surrounding tissue are loaded more than the opposite side, so that over years the face develops unevenly. Corrective practice aims to equalise that loading. Published work on chewing side preference looks at laterality, occlusal contact and bite force rather than facial shape.
Risks and caveats: Alternating the chewing side is an ordinary behaviour with no documented harms in the literature reviewed. Tooth pain, missing teeth, jaw joint problems or dentures can change which side a person chews on, and clinicians assess those causes separately.
deepLead:
Unilateral chewing correction is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person who habitually chews on one side of the mouth tries to chew on both sides, or to use the less-used side more, in the hope of reducing facial asymmetry. It is a behavioural habit change and involves no product or procedure.
Dental research has documented that many people show a consistent chewing-side preference, and has described how it relates to handedness, occlusal contact and the temporomandibular joint . A population-based German study examined self-reported chewing side preference in relation to occlusal and temporomandibular factors , and another paper has framed the preference as a form of hemispheric laterality .
No clinical study identified for this article has tested whether retraining chewing-side habits changes facial symmetry or jaw shape. The proposed link between a chewing habit and visible asymmetry therefore rests on community reasoning rather than on published trials.

name: Flipped mirror selfie check

angle.text: Users compare a mirror-reversed face with a non-reversed photo to see the face others see, since familiarity with the mirror image shapes self-perception. The idea draws on familiarity effects from psychology, while the practice itself has not been studied.

summary: Comparing a flipped and unflipped photo of your face to see how others see you; the idea rests on familiarity effects, and the practice itself is unstudied.
note: Little published research on the practice itself; the supporting ideas come from general symmetry and familiarity research.
currentQuick:
A flipped mirror selfie check means comparing the mirror view of your face, the one you see daily, with a non-mirrored or flipped photo, which is closer to how other people see you. Looksmaxxing communities use it when assessing asymmetry and angles.
The general principle that people feel more familiar with the view they see most often is described in psychology as the mere-exposure effect. No study identified here tests the flipped-selfie practice itself.
How it works: A mirror shows a left-right reversed image. Phone cameras may save either orientation. Users compare both orientations, sometimes side by side, to see which features look different. Face researchers also use left-left and right-right composites, though this method has been criticised for creating artificial features.
Risks and caveats: No physical risks. Community discussions note that comparing mirrored views can feed preoccupation with small asymmetries; this is a general observation and not a finding about this practice.
deepLead:
A flipped mirror selfie check is a looksmaxxing habit of comparing a person's mirror-reversed face with a true (non-reversed) photo. People do this because the face seen in a mirror every day differs in left-right orientation from the face others see in person or in photographs.
Facial symmetry research, which looksmaxxing communities often cite, uses fluctuating asymmetry as the main measure of left-right difference and has associated greater symmetry with higher attractiveness ratings . Psychology also describes a mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus tends to increase liking, demonstrated with faces among other stimuli .
No clinical or experimental study identified for this article has tested the flipped-selfie check as a practice.

name: Symmetry photo mirroring tools

chain: Mirror each half of the face
angle.text: Apps and editors build left-left and right-right composites from one photo so users can see exactly how their two sides differ. The composites are an established research method with known artefacts, and the visualization is immediate.

summary: Apps and editors that build left-left and right-right face composites to visualise asymmetry; a research method with known artefacts.
note: Mirrored composites can create artificial features, which researchers cite as a criticism of the method.
currentQuick:
Symmetry photo mirroring tools take a front-facing photo, split it down the midline and mirror each half to create two composite faces, one built from two left sides and one from two right sides. Users compare them with the original to see how asymmetric the face looks.
The technique is also used in academic research on facial symmetry and attractiveness, where it has been criticised for the artefacts it can produce.
How it works: The tool duplicates and flips one half of the face over a chosen midline. The result depends on where the midline is placed and on head rotation and tilt in the photo.
Risks and caveats: No physical risk. Because the composites exaggerate or hide particular features, the method has been criticised as a basis for conclusions about a face.
deepLead:
Symmetry photo mirroring tools produce composite images from a single face photograph by mirroring its left half or right half across the midline, yielding a left-left and a right-right version. Looksmaxxing communities use them to visualise asymmetry and to compare the composites with the unaltered face.
The same technique appears in facial attractiveness research, which tested the symmetry-attractiveness link by mirroring face halves and blending faces. Critics note that mirroring can create artificial features; for example a slightly bent nose can appear oversized or unnaturally small depending on which side is copied .

name: Back sleeping pillow setup

chain: Pillows keep you on your back
Less overnight pressure on one side
angle.text: Users arrange pillows to stay on their back, hoping to avoid one-sided facial pressure and uneven looks over time. No study tests this outcome, and the belief rests on forum reports about the side people sleep on.

summary: Using pillows to stay on your back at night, which looksmaxxers hope will even out one-sided facial changes; no study tests that outcome.
note: Sleep position effects on facial shape have not been studied in the sources reviewed; back sleeping is associated with positional sleep apnea in some people.
currentQuick:
A back sleeping pillow setup uses pillows placed beside the body or under the neck and knees to discourage rolling onto the side or face during sleep. Looksmaxxing users adopt it because they believe sleeping on one side contributes to facial asymmetry, wrinkles or flattening.
No published study identified here has tested whether sleep position changes facial shape. Sleep research does document health associations of different positions.
How it works: Pillows act as physical barriers or supports so the sleeper stays supine. The community theory is that continuous pressure on one side of the face during sleep affects soft tissue or skeletal development over time.
Risks and caveats: Sleep literature associates back sleeping with positional obstructive sleep apnea in a large share of OSA cases and with more frequent sleep paralysis. Positional therapy that discourages back sleeping is used for apnea.
deepLead:
A back sleeping pillow setup is an arrangement of pillows meant to keep a sleeper lying on the back instead of on one side or the stomach. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to avoid pressure on one side of the face overnight.
Users on looksmax.org have described attributing their worse-looking side to the side they sleep on, with one poster reporting acne and asymmetry concentrated on the side they favour and asking how long it takes to get used to back sleeping . Other replies in that thread attributed asymmetry to genetics .
General sleep literature describes lateral sleeping as the most common adult position, followed by back and then stomach sleeping . No study identified for this article tests pillow arrangements for changing facial appearance.

name: Chiropractic neck adjustment

angle.text: Some appearance communities seek neck adjustments for better posture and head alignment, and occasionally jaw or face alignment. Manipulation is studied for neck pain, while an appearance effect has not been shown.

summary: High-velocity neck manipulation sometimes sought for posture and jaw or face alignment; case reports link it to arterial injury and stroke.
note: Case reports describe vertebral artery dissection and other serious complications after neck manipulation.
currentQuick:
A chiropractic neck adjustment is a thrust applied to the joints of the neck, usually by a chiropractor. In looksmaxxing and related fringe circles it is sometimes discussed as a way to correct posture or alignment thought to affect the face.
Research on cervical manipulation concerns neck pain, not appearance, and its safety is debated. Published case reports describe stroke and eye bleeding after neck manipulation.
How it works: A quick, small-amplitude thrust is applied to a cervical joint, often producing a popping sound. Practitioners say it restores joint movement. Reviewers describe the evidence for effect as limited and the degree of serious risk as uncertain.
Risks and caveats: The main concern is vertebral artery dissection, which can lead to stroke. A 2001 study reported higher rates of vertebrobasilar stroke in adults under 45 who had recently visited a chiropractor, with no significant association over 45. Some chiropractors dispute a causal link.
deepLead:
A chiropractic neck adjustment, or cervical spinal manipulation, is a thrust technique applied to the joints of the neck. It is used for neck pain and is also discussed in appearance-related communities in connection with posture and head alignment.
A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence on spinal manipulation for neck pain, while a smaller body of moderate-to-low-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications . No study identified for this article evaluates neck manipulation for facial appearance.
The central safety concern is vertebral artery dissection. Case reports describe cerebellar infarction after a chiropractor's neck manipulation  and preretinal hemorrhages after high-velocity low-amplitude cervical manipulation .

name: Craniosacral therapy

chain: Light touch to skull and spine
angle.text: Some users try craniosacral therapy hoping to adjust skull bones and improve facial symmetry. The therapy rests on a claimed cranial rhythm, and reviews rate evidence for any benefit as weak.

summary: Light-touch skull and spine manipulation based on a claimed cranial rhythm; reviews find the evidence weak and the premise at odds with anatomy.
note: Medical reviews describe it as pseudoscience; the American Cancer Society advises against use on children under two.
currentQuick:
Craniosacral therapy (CST) is an alternative manual therapy in which a practitioner uses light touch on the head, spine and sacrum to detect and adjust a rhythm said to travel through the cerebrospinal fluid. A few looksmaxxing posters discuss it in connection with skull movement, occlusion and posture.
It was developed from cranial osteopathy by William Sutherland and popularised by John Upledger. Reviewers report limited evidence of benefit and describe its core assumptions as inconsistent with known anatomy.
How it works: Proponents hold that the skull bones, especially at the sphenobasilar joint, move in a cycle of flexion and extension at roughly 6 to 12 cycles per minute, and that therapists can feel and release restrictions in it. Studies have found practitioners cannot reliably identify the rhythm.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe manipulation of the skull as potentially harmful, particularly for infants and children, and report at least two deaths linked to CST spinal manipulation as of 2018. Using it as the only treatment for serious illness has been cautioned against.
deepLead:
Craniosacral therapy (CST) is a form of alternative medicine in which practitioners use light touch to feel purported rhythmic movements of the skull bones and spine and to adjust them. It grew out of cranial osteopathy devised by William Garner Sutherland in the early twentieth century, and was developed by osteopath John Upledger, who ran research on the purported pulse at Michigan State University between 1975 and 1983 .
Practitioners claim it treats conditions such as chronic pain, headaches, fibromyalgia and anxiety . Systematic reviews report limited and methodologically weak evidence, and medical reviews describe the premise as inconsistent with skull, brain and spine anatomy and physiology .
In looksmaxxing communities it appears in discussions of cranial movement, bite and posture, usually as a theory rather than a procedure with studied appearance outcomes .

name: Myofascial release / Rolfing

angle.text: Practitioners offer Rolfing and myofascial release to realign posture and the body, and in some circles the face. Trials exist for pain and function with low-certainty results, and the facial claims are untested.

summary: Hands-on fascia manipulation, best known as Rolfing, said by practitioners to realign posture and the body (and, in some circles, the face); trial evidence is thin and of low certainty.
note: No published study was found testing it for facial appearance; reviews of pain and function outcomes rate the evidence very low certainty.
currentQuick:
Rolfing, formally called Structural Integration, is a form of manual therapy created by biochemist Ida Rolf in the mid-20th century. It is usually delivered as a series of ten sessions of slow, deep pressure on connective tissue (fascia), combined with movement cues. Practitioners say it brings the body into better alignment with gravity.
In looksmaxxing discussions it appears as a fringe option, with the idea that fascia work can balance posture and facial structure. Published research has examined posture, neck function and pain rather than facial looks, and reviews describe the evidence as very low certainty.
How it works: Proponents hold that gravity and injury shorten and thicken fascia, pulling the body out of alignment, and that manual pressure lengthens it and restores balance. Researchers say this mechanism has not been validated in large controlled studies.
Risks and caveats: Sessions can be painful and leave soreness. Case reports describe harm from deep massage in unusual circumstances, such as displacement of a ureteral stent. Rolfing is not a regulated medical treatment in most places, and an Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness.
deepLead:
Rolfing, formally known as Structural Integration, is a system of manual therapy developed by the biochemist Ida P. Rolf (1896-1979) beginning in the 1940s. It is typically delivered as a ten-session series in which a practitioner applies slow, deep pressure to connective tissue (fascia) while guiding the client's movement, with the stated aim of improving alignment relative to gravity.
Myofascial release is a broader family of manual techniques that target fascia and muscle; Rolfing is the best-known branded system within it. In looksmaxxing communities, the practice is occasionally raised as a way to balance posture and, by extension, the face, though the sources reviewed for this article do not describe any practitioner organisation making specific facial-appearance claims.
Published research on Rolfing is small. A 2024 systematic review of randomized trials, as summarized by Grokipedia, characterized the evidence as very low certainty because of bias risk, small samples and inconsistent outcomes. Wikipedia notes an Australian government review in 2015 that found no clear evidence of effectiveness for Rolfing among 17 alternative therapies. No study found examined facial appearance as an outcome.

name: TMJ splint (orthotic)

angle.text: Users interested in jaw alignment discuss custom splints as a way to reposition the jaw and even out the face. Splints are used for TMJ disorders with modest, debated evidence, and appearance outcomes have not been researched.

summary: A custom dental splint worn to stabilize or reposition the jaw joint; used for TMJ disorders, with modest and debated evidence and no research on appearance outcomes.
note: Studied for jaw-joint symptoms, not for changing facial looks; repositioning splints can be followed by bite changes needing orthodontic work.
currentQuick:
A TMJ splint is a removable acrylic appliance, usually custom-made by a dentist, that fits over the upper or lower teeth. Stabilization splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to relax the jaw muscles, while repositioning splints hold the lower jaw in a different position to try to improve how the joint disc sits.
In looksmaxxing circles the idea is that correcting jaw-joint imbalance can improve bite, jaw symmetry and facial balance. Studies of splints focus on pain and joint function, and published reviews describe the evidence as modest or insufficient.
How it works: Stabilization splints are thought to reduce muscle activity and spread bite forces. Repositioning splints aim to hold the jaw forward so a displaced disc can sit better on the joint, at least while the splint is worn.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes that partial-coverage splints can cause unwanted tooth movement, and orthodontic literature describes posterior open bites after repositioning splint therapy. Splint use is generally considered reversible.
deepLead:
A TMJ splint, also called an occlusal splint, bite splint or night guard, is a removable dental appliance molded to the upper or lower teeth. It is used to protect teeth, manage temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders, stabilize the joint, or alter the bite position.
Two broad types are described. Stabilization (Michigan-type) splints sit flat against the opposing teeth to help relax jaw muscles. Repositioning splints hold the jaw in a different position, for example forward, in an attempt to improve the relationship of the joint disc.
Reviews summarized on Wikipedia report modest evidence of benefit for hard stabilization splints in TMD pain, and insufficient evidence on other points. No study found tested splints for facial appearance.

name: TMJ Botox

angle.text: Botulinum toxin in the jaw muscles is used for clenching and jaw pain, and users also seek it for a slimmer lower face or more even jaw muscles. The facial slimming is a recognized side effect of treating the masseter, and the symmetry use is off-label.

summary: Botulinum toxin injected into jaw muscles to ease temporomandibular disorders and bruxism; trials exist but results are mixed in the sources and it is off-label in most places.
note: Studied for jaw pain and disc problems, not as a proven appearance treatment; many registered trials are small or lack posted results.
currentQuick:
TMJ Botox refers to injecting botulinum toxin into jaw muscles, such as the masseter or lateral pterygoid, to calm overactive muscles in people with temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) or teeth grinding. It is a clinician-administered prescription treatment.
In looksmaxxing talk it is framed as a way to relax hyperactive jaw muscles. Wikipedia reports multiple randomized trials of lateral pterygoid injection with evidence of benefit, while a set of newer registered trials is still small and evolving.
How it works: Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at nerve endings, temporarily weakening the injected muscle. In TMD the rationale is that lateral pterygoid spasm may contribute to anterior disc displacement.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes that toxin spread can cause a fixed facial expression that resolves as the effect wears off. Effects typically last months. Use for TMD is generally off-label.
deepLead:
TMJ Botox is the use of botulinum toxin injections in the jaw muscles to treat temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD), bruxism (clenching and grinding), and related jaw pain. It is performed by clinicians and is a prescription treatment.
According to Wikipedia, injection into the lateral pterygoid muscle has been studied in multiple randomized trials with evidence of benefit, and effects typically last months. The theory behind the approach is that spasm of this muscle contributes to anterior disc displacement.
Numerous trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, including small recently completed studies, but the registry entries reviewed here do not report outcomes.
